evidence.label: A power saving for planar halving lines

headline: The maximum number of halving lines for n points in the plane is below n to the power 4/3 by a fixed margin.
scope: The result covers large even sets of points in the plane with no three on a line. The saving in the exponent is fixed but has no stated value.
plain: A halving line passes through two of n points and splits the rest evenly. Since 1998 the best upper bound on their number was about n to the power 4/3. This paper proves the power can be lowered by some fixed amount. The proof gives no value for that amount.
doesNot: This does not give a numerical value for the saving in the exponent.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: László Lovász, with an n^(3/2) upper bound
scorecard.significanceWhy: It improves an exponent that had stood since 1998 on a central problem in discrete geometry.

explanation:
Put six points at the corners of a regular hexagon. Draw the line through two of them. Ask whether it leaves the other four split evenly, two on each side. Only the three long diagonals do. Such a pair is a halving pair, and its line is a halving line[1]. Move the six points around, keeping no three on one line, and the count changes. A computer search finds six-point arrangements with six halving lines.

How many halving lines can n points have? There are about n²/2 pairs in all, but only a few can split the rest evenly. Lovász, and then Erdős, Lovász, Simmons and Straus, showed the count is at most about n to the power 3/2[4]. In 1992, Pach, Steiger and Szemerédi shaved this by a very slowly growing factor[5]. In 1998, Tamal Dey lowered the power to 4/3[6]. For a million points, n to the 4/3 is a hundred million, while n to the 3/2 is a billion.

From below, the known examples are much smaller. Erdős, Lovász, Simmons and Straus built sets with about n log n halving lines[7]. Géza Tóth, and later Gabriel Nivasch, built better ones[8]. But all known examples stay below n to any fixed power above 1[9]. So the truth lies somewhere between just over n and n to the 4/3. Later work improved smaller terms in the upper bound but kept the power 4/3[10].

This paper proves a small drop in the power. Take any large enough even set of n points, with no three on a line. It has at most C times n to the power 4/3 − ε halving lines. Here ε is one fixed number above zero, the same for every set[2]. The catch is that the proof gives no value for ε, or for C[3]. It shows a saving exists, but not how big it is.

The paper also claims a matching bound for k-sets. A k-set is a group of k points that a straight line can cut off from the rest. Dey's method bounded their number by about n times (k + 1) to the 1/3. The paper lowers that power of k by a fixed amount too[11]. This k-set bound concerns straight lines only, not curved versions of the problem[12].

The obstacle was a counting step that had looked tight. Turn a line slowly, and track which points sit below it. Points swap in and out at each halving line. Dey's crossing argument counts how many busy stretches of this sweep can fit[13]. The new proof shows that count can never be met, up to a constant, for huge sets. To do this it imagines a sequence of near-extreme examples. It then studies the shapes they approach in the limit. Positions measured by rank do not directly give real distances[15]. So the paper uses the order of the sweep directions to recover geometric control. A contradiction follows. One fixed scale then feeds a repeating argument, which yields the power saving[14].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the main bound. It says some fixed ε above zero and some C bound the halving pairs, for all large enough even sets. It also covers the related count for every rank of the sweep. The constants are not given as numbers. The k-set corollary is not named in the Lean scope note. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. Lean has checked a formal version of the halving-line bound. The saving has no stated value, the k-set corollary is outside the Lean note, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A line through two of the points that leaves the same number of other points on each side.
A group of k points that a straight line can separate from all the others.
The power in a growth rate; n to the 4/3 grows faster than n but slower than n².
A lowering of the exponent in a bound by a fixed positive amount.
A computer program that checks each step of a formally written proof.
